boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Manassas, First record (July 21, 1861) in Manassas Campaign [July 1861]. Johnston's move from the Valley, the Blackburn's Ford action of July 18, the McLean's Ford demonstration of July 21 and the retreat to Washington are context. Campaign-wide movements, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 60,680 (US 28,450; CS 32,230); the live field reads 31,680 (US 28,450; CS 3,230). Nicolay gives McDowell's command as 34,320, his moving column as 28,568 with forty-nine guns, perhaps under 28,000 after discharges, and the Confederates on the field as 32,000 with fifty-seven guns (Beauregard 21,833, Johnston 8,884, Holmes 1,355; total 32,073), plus unreported detachments. McDowell says he crossed Bull Run with about 18,000 men and that the numbers opposed were variously estimated.
claims.rationale: Figures differ in scope: command, moving column, force that crossed, and reported Confederate effectives. The live Confederate 3,230 is not adopted. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Brigadier Generals Joseph E. Johnston and P.G.T. Beauregard for the Confederates and Brigadier General Irvin McDowell for the Union; the live page lists McDowell as Major General and Johnston as Lieutenant Colonel. Nicolay says Johnston assumed command as ranking officer, and that Beauregard took personal command of the line on the plateau while Johnston returned to headquarters to watch the whole field. McDowell says he ordered the withdrawal covered and took personal command of the forces holding the Centreville ridge, and says the First Division's delay in leaving camp put the other divisions two to three hours behind. Nicolay says Miles at Centreville became incapable of duty.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a history and an interested report; the three listed commanders receive no automatic credit, and the live ranks are not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. McDowell says the retreat became a rout and then a panic, with guns and caissons abandoned at Cub Run; NPS says the Confederates were too disorganized to pursue; Nicolay says pursuit was ordered with the greatest caution and that the largest capture of guns and wagons came at the Cub Run bridge. NPS's statements on McDowell's replacement and the administration's view of a long war are campaign and political contribution, not tactical outcome.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 4,700 (US 2,950; CS 1,750); the live field reads 4,878 (US 2,896; CS 1,982). McDowell reports 19 officers and 462 men killed and 64 officers and 947 men wounded, calls the missing return very inaccurate, and says a Confederate officer admitted 1,800 killed and wounded. Nicolay gives the Union loss as 25 guns (28 claimed), 481 killed, 1,011 wounded and 1,460 wounded and other prisoners, and the Confederate loss as 387 killed and 1,582 wounded. Nicolay reports D. R. Jones's separate loss of 14 killed and 62 wounded at McLean's Ford.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The McLean's Ford figures may overlap the Confederate totals and are not added.

open_questions: Beauregard's No. 84 and Johnston's No. 81 reports on July 21, the division and brigade reports (Nos. 7-63 and 82-100+), the consolidated Union return (appendix D) and the Confederate returns remain deferred; McDowell's August 4 report year is not printed in OCR.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. John G. Nicolay's The Outbreak of Rebellion (Scribner, 1881) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, largely from the Official War Records for 1861; it quotes McDowell's and Johnston's reports and uses Beauregard's, and is not independent of the report families. McDowell's July 21-22 telegrams and his August 4 report (Official Records Series I, Volume II) are one family of interested Union accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
